prompt: Which section sets out the general obligations of an AFS licensee? One example is providing financial services efficiently and honestly and fairly.
explanation: s912A lists the licensee's general obligations. s961B is the best interests duty. s946A requires an SOA. s1041H prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct about financial products and services.

prompt: An AFS licensee becomes aware of a reportable situation. Within what period must it generally lodge a report with ASIC?
options: Within 30 days after it first knows or is reckless with respect to whether there are reasonable grounds to believe a reportable situation has arisen
Within 10 business days after the breach occurs
At the next annual compliance audit
explanation: Since 1 October 2021 the report is due within 30 days. The clock starts when the licensee first knows or is reckless with respect to whether there are reasonable grounds to believe a reportable situation has arisen. The 10 business day test was the regime before October 2021. Reporting doesn't depend on a complaint.

prompt: True or false: an AFS licensee can be required to report to ASIC about serious compliance concerns with an individual adviser authorised by a different licensee.
explanation: The breach reporting regime includes a duty to report about another licensee's relevant provider. It applies where there are reasonable grounds to believe that adviser has engaged in certain serious misconduct.

prompt: An adviser receives commissions on the life insurance they recommend. Which word are they restricted from using to describe their business?
explanation: The words 'independent' and 'impartial' and 'unbiased' are restricted if the provider receives commissions or volume-based payments or has certain conflicts. 'Financial adviser' is restricted to registered relevant providers. This adviser can be one of those.

prompt: What professional standards must a relevant provider meet under Part 7.6 Division 8A?
answer: There are four education and training standards. They are the qualifications standard and the exam standard. They also include the work and training standard (the professional year) and the CPD standard. On top of these the adviser must comply with the Code of Ethics.
keyPoints: Qualifications (education) standard: an approved qualification or the experienced provider pathway
Exam standard: pass the financial adviser exam
Work and training standard: complete the professional year
Continuing professional development (CPD) each year
Comply with the Code of Ethics
explanation: These are the professional standards for relevant providers. Registration with ASIC sits separately in Division 8C.

prompt: Which chapter of the Corporations Act 2001 regulates financial services and markets? This includes financial product advice.
explanation: Chapter 7 covers financial services and markets. That includes AFS licensing and advice obligations. Chapter 2D covers officers' duties. Chapter 5 covers external administration and Chapter 6 covers takeovers.

prompt: Which body is the external dispute resolution scheme that AFS licensees must belong to for retail client complaints?
explanation: The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) is the authorised EDR scheme. ASIC is the conduct regulator and APRA is the prudential regulator. FOS was one of the schemes AFCA replaced in 2018.

scenario: On 1 March a licensee's compliance team finds that an adviser has charged fees without valid consent since last year. By 10 March the team has reasonable grounds to believe it's a reportable situation.

extract.text: The report must be lodged with ASIC within 30 days after the financial services licensee first knows that, or is reckless with respect to whether, there are reasonable grounds to believe the reportable situation has arisen.

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.text: The 30 days runs from when the adviser first charged the fees last year.
The 30 days runs from when the licensee first knows or is reckless with respect to whether there are reasonable grounds to believe a reportable situation has arisen.
The clock can still start if the licensee is aware of a substantial risk that there are reasonable grounds but doesn't look into it. This is recklessness.
The licensee only has to report if a client complains to AFCA.

explanation: The clock is tied to the licensee's knowledge or recklessness about reasonable grounds. It is not tied to when the conduct happened. Reporting doesn't depend on a complaint. Recklessness means the licensee can't avoid the deadline by not looking.

prompt: A new client asks why you call yourself a 'financial adviser' but not 'independent'. Explain it to them in plain English.
answer: 'Financial adviser' is a protected title. Only advisers registered with ASIC who meet the professional standards can use it. 'Independent' is protected too. I can't use it because I receive commissions on life insurance. The law says anyone paid that way can't call themselves independent. The same goes for certain other benefits or ties to product issuers.
keyPoints: 'Financial adviser' is a restricted title for registered relevant providers who meet the professional standards
'Independent' is also restricted (as are 'impartial' and 'unbiased')
It can't be used by someone who receives commissions not rebated in full or volume-based payments or other benefits that could influence them. Certain ties to product issuers also rule it out
Links it to the adviser's own situation such as receiving life insurance commissions
explanation: s923A restricts 'independent' and 'impartial' and 'unbiased'. s923C restricts 'financial adviser' and 'financial planner' to relevant providers. The exam tests communication skills like this plain-English explanation.

prompt: Which section requires a Statement of Advice when personal advice is provided to a retail client?
explanation: s946A is the SOA obligation. s961B is the best interests duty. s949A is the general advice warning. s1012A covers giving a PDS when recommending a product.

prompt: When can a Record of Advice generally be used instead of a full SOA?
options: For further advice where the client's relevant circumstances and the basis of the advice aren't significantly different from earlier advice given in an SOA
Whenever the advice is about a single financial product
Whenever the client agrees in writing to waive the SOA
For any advice given over the phone
explanation: The ROA exception is for further advice that builds on a previous SOA without significant change. Product count doesn't trigger it. Neither do client waivers or the channel used.

prompt: Which of these must an SOA include?
options: Information about remuneration or commissions or other benefits that might reasonably be expected to influence the advice
A full list of the adviser's personal investment holdings
A projection guaranteeing the client's investment returns
explanation: An SOA must disclose remuneration and benefits that could influence the advice. It must also disclose interests and associations. Full personal holdings aren't required. Nor are guaranteed returns or the client's TFN.

prompt: When must an SOA generally be given to the client?
options: When the advice is provided or as soon as practicable after. In any case it must come before any further financial service arising from the advice
Within 30 days of the advice no matter when it is implemented
Only if the client asks for it in writing
Before the first meeting with the client
explanation: The SOA must be given when the advice is provided or as soon as practicable after. It must come before any further financial service arising from the advice. There is no 30-day window or on-request rule. The exception is time-critical advice under s946C(3). There the SOA can follow within 5 business days.

prompt: What warning must accompany general advice to a retail client?
answer: The advice hasn't taken into account the client's objectives or financial situation or needs. The client should consider whether it's appropriate for them. If it relates to acquiring a product they should get and read the PDS.
keyPoints: The advice doesn't take into account the client's objectives or financial situation or needs
The client should consider whether it's appropriate for them before acting
If it's about acquiring a product they should get and consider the PDS
explanation: This is the general advice warning. It reminds the client that no one has assessed their personal circumstances.

prompt: What makes financial product advice 'personal advice' rather than general advice?
options: The provider has considered one or more of the person's objectives or financial situation or needs. Or a reasonable person might expect them to have
The advice is given face to face rather than in writing
The advice recommends a specific named financial product
The client pays a fee for the advice
explanation: The test is whether the client's circumstances were considered or would reasonably be expected to have been. Delivery method doesn't decide it. Nor does naming a product or charging a fee. General advice can name products and be paid for.

prompt: Which document tells a retail client about the services offered and how the provider is paid? It also explains how to complain and comes before a financial service is provided.
explanation: The FSG explains who the provider is and what services they offer. It also covers remuneration and dispute resolution. The SOA documents personal advice. The PDS describes a product. The ROA records further advice.

prompt: True or false: for many retail financial products the client has a 14-day cooling-off period. Examples are life insurance and interests in managed investment schemes.
explanation: The cooling-off regime gives retail clients 14 days to return many products. Some products are excluded. Check the specific product.

scenario: On the phone an adviser gives a long-standing client personal advice to sell a share holding. The client says: 'Sell them right now before the market opens.' There isn't time to prepare an SOA first.

extract.text:
If:
(a) the client expressly instructs that they require a further financial service that arises out of, or is connected with, the advice to be provided immediately, or by a specified time; and
(b) it is not reasonably practicable to give the Statement of Advice to the client before that further service is provided as so instructed;
the providing entity must give the client the Statement of Advice:
(c) unless paragraph (d) applies—within 5 business days after providing that further service, or sooner if practicable; …

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.text: Because the client expressly asked for the sale immediately the adviser can sell before giving the SOA.
The SOA must then generally be given within 5 business days after the sale or sooner if practicable.
The adviser no longer needs to give an SOA at all because the advice was acted on.
Without the client's express instruction the adviser could still sell first and send the SOA within 30 days.

explanation: The general rule in s946C(1) is that the SOA comes before any further service arising from the advice. The time-critical exception needs an express client instruction. It must also be impractical to give the SOA first. Even then the SOA follows within 5 business days. There is no 30-day rule.

prompt: What's the difference between a Statement of Advice and a Record of Advice? When can a Record of Advice be used instead?
answer: An SOA is the full document for personal advice to a retail client. It sets out the advice and the basis for it. It also covers remuneration and conflicts that could influence it and any warnings. An ROA is a shorter record that can replace an SOA for further advice. It only applies where the client already received an SOA. Their relevant circumstances and the basis of the advice must not have significantly changed.
keyPoints: An SOA documents personal advice to a retail client. It includes the advice and its basis plus remuneration or conflicts that could influence it and warnings
An ROA is a record of further advice used instead of an SOA in limited cases
An ROA needs an earlier SOA to have been given to the client
The client's relevant circumstances and the basis of the advice must not be significantly different
explanation: The ROA exception saves repeating a full SOA when little has changed. Product count doesn't trigger it. Neither does the channel used or the client waiving the SOA.
source: Corps Act s946A; s946B; s947B; ASIC INFO 266

scenario: Extracts from an SOA for Priya. She asked for advice on consolidating her two super accounts.
prompt: Tap every line that has a problem.

lines.text: Statement of Advice prepared for Priya Shah.
Our advice: roll your two super accounts into Fund X and keep insurance cover equivalent to what you hold now.
Why this suits you: Fund X has had strong returns for five years. You can expect similar returns in future.
lines.issue: It presents past performance as a reliable guide to future returns. That's misleading under s1041H and Code Standard 9. It isn't a proper basis for advice.

lines.text: Fees: an advice fee of $2 200 (including GST) which you've agreed to pay.
Our practice receives a payment from Fund X for each client we refer. We don't think this affects our advice. So we haven't included the amount.
lines.issue: The SOA must disclose remuneration and benefits that might reasonably be expected to influence the advice (s947B(2)(d)). A per-referral payment from the fund is also likely conflicted remuneration (s963A).

lines.text: You told us you weren't sure of your current insurance details. This advice may be based on incomplete information. Consider whether it's appropriate before acting.

explanation: The last line is a correct s961H warning and not a problem. The two issues are a misleading basis for the advice and missing remuneration that is probably banned anyway.
source: Corps Act s947B(2); s961H; s963A; s1041H; Code of Ethics Standard 9

scenario: At a public seminar an adviser says: 'Most people in their 40s should think about salary sacrificing into super.' Afterwards an attendee shows him her payslip. She asks if she should salary sacrifice $500 a month. He looks at her income and says yes.
prompt: How should the two statements be classified?
options: The seminar comment was general advice. The answer to the attendee was personal advice so personal advice obligations apply to it
Both were general advice because no SOA was prepared
Both were personal advice because the adviser is a registered relevant provider
Neither was financial product advice because no specific fund was named
explanation: Advice becomes personal when the provider has considered the person's objectives or financial situation or needs. It is also personal if a reasonable person would expect them to have. Looking at her payslip does that. Whether an SOA was prepared doesn't change the classification. Advice about super contributions is financial product advice even if no fund is named.
source: Corps Act s766B(3); s766B(4); ASIC RG 244

prompt: Which of these is most likely to be conflicted remuneration?
options: A bonus from a platform provider based on how much client money the adviser places on that platform
A fee the client agrees to pay directly for the advice
A fixed salary that isn't linked to which products are recommended
Reimbursement of a client-agreed fee deducted from the client's account
explanation: Conflicted remuneration is a benefit that could reasonably be expected to influence the product recommended or the advice given. Volume-based payments from product providers are the classic example. Fees paid by the client aren't.

extract.text:
Conflicted remuneration means any benefit, whether monetary or non‑monetary, given to a financial services licensee, or a representative of a financial services licensee, who provides financial product advice to persons as retail clients that:
(a) because of the nature of the benefit or the circumstances in which it is given:
(i) could reasonably be expected to influence the choice of financial product recommended by the licensee or representative to retail clients; or
(ii) could reasonably be expected to influence the financial product advice given to retail clients by the licensee or representative; and
(b) is not given to the licensee or representative by a person who is a retail client in relation to a financial product or financial service provided by the licensee or representative to the client.

prompt: True or false: all commissions on life risk insurance products are banned for financial advisers.
explanation: Life risk insurance commissions are an exception to the conflicted remuneration ban. But the exception has conditions. The commission must be level or meet ASIC's benefit ratio and clawback requirements. Under s963BB the client must also give informed consent to the commission before the policy is issued.
source: Corps Act s963B(1)(b); s963BB; ASIC Corporations (Life Insurance Commissions) Instrument 2017/510

prompt: Under ASIC's life insurance commission rules what are the maximum upfront and ongoing commission caps?
explanation: Since 2020 upfront commissions are capped at 60% of the first year's premium. Ongoing commissions are capped at 20%. Both caps exclude GST. Commissions are also clawed back if a policy ends in its first two years.

prompt: Can an adviser charge a percentage-based (asset-based) fee on money a client borrowed to invest?
answer: No. Asset-based fees on borrowed amounts are banned when giving personal advice to retail clients.
keyPoints: No. It's banned
The ban covers asset-based fees on the borrowed amount
It applies when giving personal advice to retail clients
explanation: The ban stops advisers profiting from recommending gearing. s964D applies it to licensees and s964E to authorised representatives. It doesn't apply if it isn't reasonably apparent that the amount was borrowed. That exception doesn't reduce the duty to make reasonable inquiries.

prompt: A client has an ongoing fee arrangement. What does the law require for it to keep running each year?
options: The client's written consent to the arrangement continuing and to the fees
Nothing; it continues until the client cancels
explanation: Ongoing fee arrangements need the client's signed and dated consent to renew each year. The 2024 reforms replaced the old renewal notice and fee disclosure statement with this single annual consent. The consent window opens 60 days before the agreed reference day and closes 150 days after it.
source: Corps Act Part 7.7A Div 3; ASIC INFO 286

scenario: An adviser recommends a retail life insurance policy (not held through super) and will receive an upfront commission from the insurer.

extract.text:
… paragraphs 963B(1)(a), (b) and (ba) do not apply to a monetary benefit given in connection with the issue or sale of the relevant product to the client unless:
(b) before the issue or sale of the relevant product, the client consented to the monetary benefit being given; and
(c) before the consent was given, the following information was disclosed to the client: …
(iii) for a life risk insurance product or consumer credit insurance—the rate of the monetary benefit, expressed as a percentage of the policy cost payable for the product; …
(vii) the fact that the consent is irrevocable; …

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.text: The commission is only exempt from the ban if it is level or meets ASIC's benefit ratio and clawback requirements.
Before the policy is issued the client must consent to the commission after being told its rate as a percentage of the policy cost.
The client can withdraw that consent at any time and stop the commission.
Disclosing the commission in the SOA is enough on its own.

explanation: Life risk commissions are only permitted as level commission or within the benefit ratio and clawback rules in Instrument 2017/510. Since the DBFO reforms they also need the client's prior informed consent. That consent is irrevocable. Disclosure in the SOA doesn't replace it.
source: Corps Act s963B(1)(b); s963BB; ASIC Corporations (Life Insurance Commissions) Instrument 2017/510

prompt: Why is a volume-based bonus from a product issuer conflicted remuneration when an advice fee the client pays you isn't?
answer: Conflicted remuneration is a benefit that could reasonably be expected to influence which product you recommend or the advice you give. A volume bonus rewards putting more client money into that product. So it could influence you. The definition excludes benefits given by the retail client. So client-paid fees aren't conflicted remuneration. They still need consent and must be fair and reasonable.
keyPoints: Conflicted remuneration is a benefit that could reasonably be expected to influence the product recommended or the advice given
A volume bonus rewards placing more money in a product. So it could influence the recommendation
Benefits given by the retail client are excluded from the definition
Client-paid fees still need proper consent and must be fair and reasonable and value for money
explanation: The test in s963A is about the nature of the benefit and who gives it. Code Standard 7 still applies to client-paid fees.
source: Corps Act s963A; Code of Ethics Standard 7

scenario: A client tells her adviser she's taking out a $200 000 margin loan to add to her $300 000 portfolio. The adviser's agreement charges 1% a year of the total portfolio value.

extract.text:
(1) The financial services licensee must not charge an asset‑based fee on a borrowed amount used or to be used to acquire financial products by or on behalf of the client.
(3) Subsections (1) and (2) do not apply in relation to a borrowed amount if it is not reasonably apparent that the amount has been borrowed.

prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: The 1% fee can't be charged on the $200 000 that was borrowed
The fee is fine as long as it's disclosed in the SOA
The fee is fine if the client consents to it in writing
The ban applies to licensees but not to authorised representatives
explanation: The client told the adviser about the loan. So it's reasonably apparent the money is borrowed and the exception in s964D(3) doesn't help. Disclosure and consent don't cure a banned fee. s964E applies the same ban to authorised representatives.

prompt: Before a reporting entity provides a designated service to a new customer what does the AML/CTF Act generally require?
options: Customer due diligence that includes verifying the customer's identity
A credit check on the customer
Collecting the customer's tax file number
explanation: The customer must be identified and their identity verified before the designated service is provided. From 31 March 2026 the Act calls this initial customer due diligence. It used to be the applicable customer identification procedure. Threshold transaction reports relate to physical cash of $10 000 or more. Credit checks and TFNs aren't AML/CTF requirements.

prompt: An adviser's licensee has lodged a suspicious matter report about a client. The client asks if anything is wrong. What must the adviser not do?
options: Tell the client that a suspicious matter report has been made
Continue to keep records of the client's transactions
Talk to the licensee's AML/CTF compliance officer
Answer general questions about the client's portfolio
explanation: Since 31 March 2025 the tipping off offence prohibits disclosing SMR information where the disclosure would or could reasonably be expected to prejudice an investigation. Telling the client an SMR was lodged is the classic example. Keeping records is fine. So is talking to your AML/CTF compliance officer and giving normal portfolio service.

prompt: Which Australian Privacy Principle requires an entity to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse and loss and unauthorised access?
explanation: APP 11 is security of personal information. APP 1 is open and transparent management. APP 6 is use or disclosure. APP 12 is access to personal information.

prompt: True or false: if an eligible data breach occurs the entity must notify the individuals at risk of serious harm and the OAIC.
explanation: The Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires notifying affected individuals and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.

prompt: What is a tax (financial) advice service?
answer: Tax advice given in the course of financial advice of a kind usually given by a financial services licensee or relevant provider. The client can reasonably be expected to rely on it for tax purposes. An example is the tax consequences of a recommended strategy.
keyPoints: Tax advice given as part of financial advice of a kind a licensee or relevant provider usually gives
It's about the client's liabilities or obligations or entitlements under a tax law
The client can reasonably be expected to rely on it for tax purposes
explanation: Relevant providers who give these services must meet the TASA requirements. Subdivision 50-AA sets out civil penalties for breaches.
source: TASA s90-15; Subdiv 50-AA; TPB Information Sheet 20/2014; ASIC INFO 268

scenario: A licensee has lodged a suspicious matter report about a client's unusual cash deposits. The client rings the adviser to ask about their portfolio.

extract.text:
(b) the person discloses information to another person (other than an AUSTRAC entrusted person); and
(c) the information is covered by subsection (2); and
(d) the disclosure of the information would or could reasonably be expected to prejudice an investigation: …

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.text: Telling the client 'we've had to report you to AUSTRAC' could be an offence.
Discussing the report with an AUSTRAC entrusted person is not tipping off.
The adviser must refuse to discuss the client's portfolio at all.
The test is whether the disclosure would or could reasonably be expected to prejudice an investigation.

explanation: Since 31 March 2025 the offence turns on whether disclosing SMR information would or could reasonably be expected to prejudice an investigation. Normal service can continue. Disclosures to AUSTRAC entrusted persons are carved out.

prompt: So staff can work from home your practice emails unencrypted client fact finds to staff's personal Gmail accounts. Which privacy obligation does this engage and what should change?
answer: APP 11 applies. The practice must take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse and interference and loss. It must also protect it from unauthorised access or modification or disclosure. Sending fact finds to personal email isn't reasonable. Use secure systems the practice controls instead. If information is compromised and serious harm is likely the notifiable data breaches scheme applies.
keyPoints: APP 11: take reasonable steps to protect the personal information held
Protect it from misuse and interference and loss as well as unauthorised access or modification or disclosure
Change to secure systems the practice controls (such as encryption and approved platforms) instead of personal email
If a breach is likely to cause serious harm the notifiable data breaches scheme applies
explanation: Fact finds hold sensitive financial and often health information. The standard is what's reasonable in the circumstances. That standard rises with sensitivity.
source: Privacy Act Sch 1 APP 11.1; Part IIIC

scenario: An adviser's laptop holding unencrypted client files is stolen from her car. The practice assesses that serious harm to the clients is likely and can't be prevented by remedial action.
prompt: What must the practice do?
options: Notify the affected individuals and the OAIC as soon as practicable
Notify only its professional indemnity insurer
Nothing because a third party committed the crime
Notify clients only if they ask what happened
explanation: This is an eligible data breach. Unauthorised access is likely to result in serious harm and remedial action can't prevent it. The entity must prepare a statement for the Commissioner and notify affected individuals as soon as practicable. Who caused the breach doesn't matter.
source: Privacy Act Part IIIC (s26WE; s26WK; s26WL)

prompt: Which section of the Corporations Act sets out the duty to act in the client's best interests?
explanation: s961B is the best interests duty. s961J is the priority rule. s946A relates to SOAs. s912A sets the general obligations of licensees.

prompt: What does the priority rule require?
answer: Sometimes the client's interests conflict with the interests of the adviser or their licensee or associates. If the adviser knows about the conflict or reasonably ought to know about it then they must give priority to the client's interests.
keyPoints: There is a conflict between the client's interests and those of the adviser or licensee or their associates
The adviser knows or reasonably ought to know about the conflict
The adviser must give priority to the client's interests
explanation: This sits alongside the best interests duty and the appropriate advice requirement.

prompt: Which section requires the advice itself to be appropriate to the client as if the best interests duty had been met?
explanation: s961G is the appropriate advice requirement. s961B is the best interests duty. s961H covers warnings where advice relies on incomplete or inaccurate information. s961J is the priority rule.

prompt: Which of these is a step in the 'safe harbour' for the best interests duty?
options: Identify the client's objectives and financial situation and needs disclosed through their instructions
Recommend at least two alternative products for comparison
Obtain the licensee's written approval before giving the advice
Give the client a Statement of Advice within 24 hours
explanation: Identifying the client's objectives and financial situation and needs is the first safe harbour step. The other options sound procedural but are not safe harbour steps. SOA timing is dealt with separately.

prompt: While the adviser is giving personal advice it becomes reasonably apparent that the client's information about their circumstances is incomplete or inaccurate. What must the adviser do?
options: Warn the client that the advice is based on incomplete or inaccurate information and that they should consider whether it is appropriate
Refuse to give any advice until the information is complete
Give a Record of Advice instead of a Statement of Advice
explanation: s961H requires a warning. It does not require a refusal. The ROA option confuses disclosure documents. There is no ASIC notification requirement here.

extract.text:
(1) If it is reasonably apparent that information relating to the objectives, financial situation and needs of the client on which the advice is based is incomplete or inaccurate, the provider must, in accordance with subsections (2) and (3), warn the client that:
(a) the advice is, or may be, based on incomplete or inaccurate information relating to the client’s relevant personal circumstances; and
(b) because of that, the client should, before acting on the advice, consider the appropriateness of the advice, having regard to the client’s objectives, financial situation and needs.
(2) The warning must be given to the client at the same time as the advice is provided and, subject to subsection (3), by the same means as the advice is provided.

prompt: An adviser recommends their licensee's in-house fund because the licensee rewards in-house sales. A comparable external fund is cheaper for the client. Which obligation is most directly breached?
explanation: The adviser has put the licensee's interests ahead of the client's in a known conflict. Disclosure documents do not cure that. The priority rule requires putting the client first.

prompt: A client asks about a complex aged care strategy that is outside the adviser's expertise. What does the safe harbour expect?
options: Decline to give advice on that subject matter and consider referring the client
Give the advice with a general advice warning
Give the advice but in an ROA rather than an SOA
Give the advice as long as the licensee is authorised for it
explanation: One safe harbour step is to decline advice that is outside the adviser's expertise. Knowing when to refer is also a listed learning outcome for the exam.
source: Corps Act s961B(2); ASIC exam preparation guidance

prompt: A client asks you only whether to switch super funds. What does the safe harbour require you to do before recommending a switch?
answer: First I identify the objectives and financial situation and needs she has told me about. I identify the subject matter (her super) and her circumstances that are relevant to it. Insurance in her current fund is one example. I make reasonable inquiries if anything seems incomplete or inaccurate. I check that I have the expertise and decline if I do not. I reasonably investigate and assess suitable funds. I base every judgement on her relevant circumstances. I also take any other step that is reasonably in her best interests.
keyPoints: Identify the objectives and financial situation and needs the client disclosed
Identify the subject matter sought and the client's relevant circumstances
Make reasonable inquiries where information is reasonably apparent to be incomplete or inaccurate
Assess whether you have the expertise and decline if not
Reasonably investigate and assess suitable products and base all judgements on the client's relevant circumstances
explanation: These map to s961B(2)(a) to (f). Step (g) sits on top: any other step reasonably regarded as in the client's best interests. For a fund switch the classic relevant circumstances are loss of insurance and fees.

extract.text: A reasonable investigation into the financial products that might achieve those of the objectives and meet those of the needs of the client that would reasonably be considered relevant to advice on the subject matter sought by the client does not require an investigation into every financial product available.

prompt: Which of these is NOT required by the safe harbour in s961B(2)?
options: Investigating every financial product available on the market
Making reasonable inquiries where information is reasonably apparent to be incomplete or inaccurate
Assessing whether you have the expertise to advise on the subject matter
Basing all judgements on the client's relevant circumstances
explanation: The investigation must be reasonable. s961D(1) says that does not mean every product available. If the client asks you to consider a specific product then it must be included (s961D(2)). The other three options are safe harbour steps (c) and (d) and (f).

scenario: A client won't give details of a large loan on an investment property. They say it is 'not relevant'. The adviser goes ahead with advice on super contributions.

extract.text:
(2) The warning must be given to the client at the same time as the advice is provided and, subject to subsection (3), by the same means as the advice is provided.
(3) If a Statement of Advice is the means by which the advice is provided, or is given to the client at the same time as the advice is provided, the warning may be given by including it in the Statement of Advice.
(5) Nothing in this section affects the duty of the provider under section 961B to make reasonable inquiries to obtain complete and accurate information.

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.text: The adviser must warn that the advice is or may be based on incomplete information.
If the advice is given in the SOA then the warning can be included in the SOA.
Once the warning is given the adviser no longer needs to make reasonable inquiries.
The warning can be sent a week after the advice.

explanation: The warning is in addition to the duty to make reasonable inquiries. It does not replace it. The warning must be given at the same time as the advice. It must also be given by the same means unless the SOA carries it.

prompt: What's the difference between the best interests duty (s961B) and the appropriate advice requirement (s961G)?
answer: s961B is about how you advise. You must act in the client's best interests and you can show this by following the safe harbour steps. s961G is about the result. You may only give the advice if it would be reasonable to conclude it is appropriate to the client had you met s961B. Both apply. A good process does not save advice that is not appropriate.
keyPoints: s961B is about the process of acting in the client's best interests (the safe harbour is one way to show it)
s961G is about the outcome: the advice itself must be appropriate to the client
s961G tests appropriateness as if s961B had been met
Both apply: meeting one does not satisfy the other
explanation: The exam often describes a sound process that ends in an unsuitable recommendation. It also describes the reverse. Name the obligation that fails.

scenario: An adviser's file note for Sam (45). He wants to consolidate three super funds.
prompt: Tap every line that shows a problem.

lines.text: Sam wants one super fund instead of three with lower total fees.
Sam's current fund has death and TPD cover he relies on. I didn't check whether the new fund offers equivalent cover.
lines.issue: Insurance is a relevant circumstance for a fund switch. Not checking it fails the safe harbour steps on relevant circumstances and reasonable investigation (s961B(2)(b) and (e) and (f)).

lines.text: Recommended our in-house fund because the practice gets a higher platform bonus for it. A cheaper external fund was comparable.
lines.issue: This puts the practice's interests ahead of Sam's (priority rule in s961J). The bonus is also likely conflicted remuneration (s963A).

lines.text: Compared the recommended fund's fees with Sam's three current funds.
Sam said he didn't understand the investment options. I didn't explain them because it would take too long.
lines.issue: Code Standard 5 requires you to be satisfied on reasonable grounds that the client understands the advice. This includes the benefits and costs and risks of the products.

lines.text: Gave Sam his SOA before arranging the rollover.

explanation: Three lines fail. Insurance was not investigated. A conflict was resolved in the practice's favour. There was no check that the client understood. Comparing fees and giving the SOA before implementing are both right.
source: Corps Act s961B(2); s961J; s963A; Code of Ethics Standard 5

prompt: A client asks what 'acting in my best interests' actually means for them. Explain it in plain English.
answer: It means I start by understanding your goals and situation and needs. I ask more questions if something is missing. I only advise on things I have the expertise for and I refer you if I don't. My recommendations must be based on your circumstances and be appropriate for you. If what is good for me or my licensee conflicts with what is good for you then you come first.
keyPoints: Understand the client's goals and situation and needs and ask more if something is missing
Only advise within your expertise or refer
Recommendations are based on the client's circumstances and must be appropriate for them
If interests conflict the client's interests come first
explanation: This covers s961B and s961G and s961J without jargon. Communication is part of the learning outcomes for the ethics area.

prompt: How many standards are in the Financial Planners and Advisers Code of Ethics 2019?
explanation: The Code has 12 standards. 5 is the number of values: trustworthiness / competence / honesty / fairness / diligence.
source: Financial Planners and Advisers Code of Ethics 2019

prompt: Which standard says you must not advise or refer or act in any other manner where you have a conflict of interest or duty?
explanation: Standard 3 is the conflicts standard. Standard 1 is acting in line with the law. Standard 2 is acting with integrity and in the client's best interests. Standard 6 is considering the broad effects of advice.

prompt: Which of these is one of the five values in the Code of Ethics?
explanation: The five values are trustworthiness / competence / honesty / fairness / diligence. Efficiency appears in s912A but is not one of the Code's values. Loyalty and profitability are not listed.

prompt: Under Standard 7 what is required before you receive a fee or benefit from a client?
options: The client's free, prior and informed consent. The fee must also be fair and reasonable and represent value for money
Written approval from your licensee only
Disclosure of the fee in the general advice warning
Nothing as long as the fee is disclosed in the SOA
explanation: Standard 7 needs both informed consent and a fee that is fair and reasonable and represents value for money. Licensee approval or SOA disclosure on its own is not enough.

prompt: What does Standard 6 require?
answer: Take into account the broad effects arising from the client acting on your advice. Actively consider the client's broader long-term interests and likely circumstances.
keyPoints: Consider the broad effects of the client acting on the advice
Actively consider the client's broader long-term interests
Consider the client's likely circumstances and not just their current ones
explanation: Standard 6 looks past the immediate recommendation to the client's whole situation over time.

prompt: True or false: advice can meet every requirement of the Corporations Act and still breach the Code of Ethics.
explanation: The Code sets standards above the legal minimum. Spotting scenarios that are lawful but don't comply with the Code is a listed exam learning outcome.
source: Code of Ethics; ASIC exam preparation guidance

prompt: Which Code of Ethics standard requires you to keep complete and accurate records of advice and services provided?
explanation: Standard 8 covers records. Standard 4 is acting only with the client's free, prior and informed consent. Standard 10 is knowledge and skills. Standard 12 is upholding the profession's standards.

prompt: Which ethical approach asks which option will produce the most good and do the least harm for everyone affected?
explanation: The utilitarian approach weighs outcomes. The rights approach protects people's moral rights. The justice approach asks about fair treatment. The virtue approach asks what a person of good character would do.
source: Markkula Center for Applied Ethics: A framework for ethical decision making

prompt: Under Standard 4 when may you act for a client?
options: Only with the client's free, prior and informed consent
Whenever acting is in the licensee's interests
Once the client has signed the FSG
Whenever the client has been given an SOA
explanation: Standard 4 requires consent that is free, prior and informed. Receiving a document is not the same as informed consent.

scenario: A client pays an ongoing advice fee of $3 300 a year. Each year they sign a valid annual consent. In return they get one automated email a year and no review meeting.

extract.text: You must satisfy yourself that any fees and charges that the client must pay to you or your principal, and any benefits that you or your principal receive, in connection with acting for the client are fair and reasonable and represent value for money for the client.

prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.text: A valid annual consent means the fee automatically complies with the Code.
The adviser must be satisfied the fee is fair and reasonable and represents value for money.
The arrangement could meet the Corporations Act consent rules and still breach the Code.
Standard 7 bans ongoing fees altogether.

explanation: The Code sits above the law. Annual consent satisfies the Corporations Act requirements. Standard 7 separately requires value for money. That is doubtful when almost no service is delivered.
source: Code of Ethics Standard 7; Corps Act Part 7.7A Div 3; ASIC INFO 286

prompt: A client asks you to backdate a file note so it shows a risk discussion that never happened. Use at least two ethical frameworks to explain why you refuse. Then say what you would do.
answer: Rights approach: backdating deceives everyone who relies on the file. That includes the licensee and AFCA and ASIC. It also breaks my duty of honesty. Utilitarian approach: the client's short-term benefit is outweighed by the harm. Everyone who relies on accurate records is harmed and so is trust in the profession. Virtue approach: an honest professional would not do it. Standard 8 requires complete and accurate records. I would refuse and explain why. Then I would record the request.
keyPoints: Names and correctly applies at least two frameworks (such as utilitarian or rights or justice or common good or virtue)
Backdating creates false records: Standard 8 requires records to be complete and accurate
Recognises it is dishonest and undermines trust (the values of honesty and trustworthiness)
Ends with a clear action: refuse and explain and document the request
explanation: The exam asks you to apply more than one framework to the same dilemma. When different frameworks reach the same answer the decision is stronger.
source: Markkula Center: A framework for ethical decision making; Code of Ethics values and Standard 8

scenario: An adviser's notes after meetings with Tom and Ana. They are a couple in their 50s.
prompt: Tap every line that breaches the Code of Ethics.

lines.text: Explained my services and fees and got their signed consent before starting work.
Recommended they withdraw $80 000 from super to clear their car loan. I didn't look at the effect on their retirement because they only asked about debt.
lines.issue: Standard 6 requires you to consider the broad effects of acting on the advice and the client's long-term interests. This applies even when advice is scaled.

lines.text: Tom seemed confused about the product's risks. I didn't go into it because Ana understood.
lines.issue: Standard 5: you must be satisfied that each client understands the advice. This includes the product's benefits and costs and risks.

lines.text: Accepted concert tickets from the provider of the fund I recommended.
lines.issue: Standard 7: you may not receive benefits from a third party other than your principal unless the Corporations Act expressly permits it. It is also a conflict under Standard 3.

lines.text: Saved the fact find and meeting notes and copies of all documents they gave me to their file.

explanation: Getting consent first (Standard 4) is right. Keeping complete records (Standard 8) is also right. The breaches concern broad effects and client understanding and a third-party benefit.

prompt: A client asks why you need their signed consent to fees when they've already said yes on the phone. Explain in plain English.
answer: The Code says your consent has to be free, prior and informed. That means you give it before I charge and without pressure. You also know exactly what you are paying and why. It covers everything I am paid for acting for you. For some fees the law also requires your written and signed consent. An ongoing fee is one example and that consent is renewed each year. Separately I have to be satisfied the fee is fair and good value for you.
keyPoints: Consent must be free, prior and informed: before charging and without pressure and knowing what it is for
It covers all benefits the adviser receives for acting for the client including fees
The law requires written and signed consent for some fees such as ongoing fees renewed each year
The adviser must also be satisfied the fee is fair and reasonable and value for money
explanation: This combines Code Standards 4 and 7 with the Corporations Act consent rules for ongoing fees.
source: Code of Ethics Standards 4 and 7; Corps Act Part 7.7A Div 3; ASIC INFO 286

prompt: What is scaled advice?
answer: Scaled advice is personal advice limited to particular subject matter. The adviser and the client agree on that scope. The best interests duty still applies to the advice within it.
keyPoints: It's still personal advice
Its scope is limited to particular subject matter
The scope is agreed between adviser and client
The best interests duty still applies to the advice within that scope
explanation: ASIC's guidance explains how to scale advice and still meet the best interests duty and related obligations.

prompt: A 63-year-old client with low risk tolerance needs to start drawing an income in two years. The adviser recommends a geared portfolio of 100% growth assets. What is the main problem?
options: The advice doesn't suit the client's risk tolerance and time horizon or their income needs
The adviser should have given an ROA instead of an SOA
Growth assets can't be recommended to anyone over 60
The general advice warning was missing
explanation: The strategy clashes with the client's risk profile and short timeframe. So it fails the appropriateness and best interests tests. There's no age ban on growth assets. Personal advice needs an SOA rather than a general advice warning.
source: Corps Act s961B; s961G; ASIC RG 175

prompt: Poor investment returns just before or early in retirement can do far more damage than the same returns earlier in life. What is this risk called?
explanation: Sequencing risk is about the order of returns when balances are largest. Longevity risk is outliving your savings. Inflation risk is losing purchasing power. Liquidity risk is not being able to access money when you need it.
source: Iskra & Smark (2017); Financial Planning Research Journal (ASIC reading list)

prompt: A client has a secure income and large assets. But they become very anxious about any short-term loss. How would you describe their risk profile?
options: High risk capacity and low risk tolerance
Low risk capacity and high risk tolerance
High risk capacity and high risk tolerance
Low risk capacity and low risk tolerance
explanation: Risk capacity is the financial ability to absorb losses. Risk tolerance is the willingness to accept them. Advice should consider both.
source: Hunt (2016); Investment risk profiling; Financial Planning Research Journal (ASIC reading list)

prompt: True or false: agreeing to scale advice to a single topic removes the best interests duty for that advice.
explanation: Scaling narrows the subject matter. The best interests duty and related obligations still apply to the advice given. The adviser must also consider whether the scope is reasonable.

prompt: Which ASIC regulatory guide contains an example Statement of Advice for scaled advice to a new client?
explanation: RG 90 is the example SOA. RG 78 covers breach reporting. RG 146 was the old adviser training guide. RG 246 covers conflicted remuneration.

scenario: A client wants advice only on whether to make extra contributions to super. In the fact find the adviser notices $25 000 of credit card debt at 20% interest.
prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.text: The adviser can scale the advice to super contributions if that scope is reasonable.
Because the advice is scaled the adviser can ignore the credit card debt completely.
The best interests duty still applies to the scaled advice.
Scaled advice doesn't need a Statement of Advice.

explanation: Scaling narrows the subject matter but not the duties. High-interest debt is a relevant circumstance for whether extra contributions are in the client's interests. So it must at least be considered and discussed. Scaled personal advice still needs an SOA.
source: Corps Act s961B; s946A; ASIC RG 244; INFO 267

prompt: What's the difference between risk tolerance and risk capacity? Why does advice need both?
answer: Risk tolerance is willingness. It's how comfortable the client is with ups and downs and losses. Risk capacity is ability. It's how much loss their finances can absorb without derailing their goals. The two can point in different directions. A wealthy client may panic at small losses. A keen client may not be able to afford any. Advice needs to account for both.
keyPoints: Risk tolerance is the client's willingness to accept volatility and loss
Risk capacity is their financial ability to absorb losses without harming their goals
The two can differ (for example high capacity but low tolerance)
Suitable advice takes both into account
explanation: Hunt (2016) on the ASIC reading list covers the psychology of risk profiling. Questionnaires often measure tolerance only.
source: Hunt (2016); Investment risk profiling: Lessons from psychology; Financial Planning Research Journal

scenario: Mei is 42. She took ten years out of paid work to care for her children and now works part time. Her super balance is far below her partner's.
prompt: Which strategy most directly addresses the gap in her super?
options: Contribution splitting or spouse contributions from her partner if eligible
Switching her super to a high-growth option to 'catch up'
Delaying any super advice until she returns to full-time work
Withdrawing her super early to pay down the mortgage
explanation: Splitting and spouse contributions move savings to the partner with the lower balance. That directly targets the gap that career breaks create. A growth switch might be part of advice. But chasing returns ignores her risk profile. Delaying wastes time. Early access generally isn't available.
source: Craft et al. (2018); Retirement outcomes for female primary carers in Australia; Financial Planning Research Journal; ATO rules on contribution splitting and spouse contributions

prompt: Explain sequencing risk in plain English to a 64-year-old client who's about to retire.
answer: It's not just how much your investments earn on average. It's also when the good and bad years happen. A big fall just before or early in retirement hurts most. That's when your balance is at its largest and you're starting to draw on it. Selling to fund your income in a downturn locks the losses in. We can manage it. For example we can hold a cash buffer for the next couple of years of income.
keyPoints: The order of returns matters as well as the average
Losses just before or early in retirement do the most damage because the balance is largest
Drawing income in a downturn locks in losses
Gives a way to manage it (for example a cash buffer or a lower-risk allocation for near-term income)
explanation: Iskra & Smark (2017) on the ASIC extension list covers sequencing risk for baby boomers.
source: Iskra & Smark (2017); Sequencing risk for baby boomers; Financial Planning Research Journal

prompt: A client won't sell a share that has fallen 40% because selling would 'lock in' the loss. Which bias does this best show?
explanation: Losses feel worse than equal gains feel good. So the client avoids realising one. Herding is following the crowd. Overconfidence is overrating your own judgement. Recency bias overweights recent events.

prompt: A client insists their home is worth $900k because a neighbour's sold for that two years ago. Recent sales have been lower. Which bias is this?
explanation: The client is fixed on an initial reference number. Mental accounting is about labelling money. Framing is about how a choice is presented. Status quo bias is a preference for not changing.

prompt: A client spends their tax refund on a holiday while carrying a credit card balance at 20% interest. Which bias best explains this?
explanation: The refund is treated as 'bonus' money in a separate mental account. Yet paying down the debt is worth more. The other biases don't explain treating money differently by its source.

prompt: A client wants to buy a cryptocurrency because 'everyone at work is in it'. Which bias is this?
explanation: Herding is copying what others do instead of doing your own analysis. Home bias is favouring domestic assets. Status quo bias is resisting change. Anchoring is fixing on a reference point.
source: Pompian (2012); Behavioural finance and investor types (ASIC reading list)

prompt: What is overconfidence bias? How does it tend to show up in investors?
answer: It's overestimating your own knowledge or your ability to predict outcomes. It shows up as excessive trading and concentrated portfolios. It also shows up as underestimating risk.
keyPoints: Overestimating your own knowledge or skill or ability to predict outcomes
Shows up as excessive trading
Shows up as concentrated portfolios and underestimating risk
explanation: Studies of retail brokerage accounts found the most active traders earned the lowest net returns.

prompt: An adviser settles on a strategy early. They then give more weight to research that supports it and dismiss research that doesn't. Which bias is the adviser showing?
explanation: Confirmation bias is favouring information that supports an existing view. The exam expects you to spot biases in advisers as well as clients.

prompt: A client accepts a strategy described as having a '90% chance of preserving capital'. They reject the same strategy described as having a '10% chance of loss'. Which effect is this?
explanation: The outcome is identical. Only the presentation changed. Advisers need to present risk in balanced ways.

prompt: True or false: present bias helps explain why people under-save for retirement. Present bias is the tendency to favour rewards now over larger rewards later.
explanation: Present bias makes future benefits feel smaller than they are. So saving loses out to spending today.

prompt: A client refuses to sell a poor investment because it's 'still down 30% from what I paid'. How would you respond?
answer: Recognise loss aversion: losses feel worse than equal gains feel good. Reframe the decision around the investment's future prospects and the client's goals. The purchase price doesn't matter because the loss has already happened whether or not they sell. Look at the whole portfolio rather than one holding. It's still their decision. So record the advice and their reasons.
keyPoints: Names the bias: loss aversion (losses feel worse than equal gains)
Reframes around future prospects instead of the purchase price: the loss has already happened
Looks at the whole portfolio and the client's goals
Respects the client's decision but documents the advice and reasons
explanation: The exam asks you to spot a bias and respond to it appropriately. Respecting client autonomy while recording advice ties in with Standard 8.

prompt: Decide whether each statement about biases is true or false.

statements.text: Advisers can show confirmation bias in their own research.
Herding only affects clients and never advisers.
Describing the same strategy as a '90% chance of no loss' rather than a '10% chance of loss' can change a client's decision.
Present bias makes future rewards feel larger than they really are.

explanation: Biases affect advisers too. Examples are confirmation bias in research and herding into popular products. Framing changes decisions even when outcomes are identical. Present bias makes future rewards feel smaller. That's why people under-save.
source: Pompian (2012); Tversky & Kahneman (1981); ASIC exam preparation guidance

scenario: A client measures every review against their portfolio's peak value in 2021. The portfolio has grown strongly over the last two years. Yet they keep saying they've 'lost money'.
prompt: Which bias is the client showing?
explanation: The client is fixed on one reference point (the 2021 peak) and judges everything against it. Herding is following others. Mental accounting is treating money differently by label. Overconfidence is overrating your own judgement.
source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974); heuristics and biases; Pompian (2012)
